questions.text: A fraud model achieves 98% accuracy on a dataset where 2% of claims are fraudulent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model has learned to detect fraud very effectively
The model always predicts 'not fraud', matching the 98% majority class
The model is overfitting to the training data
98% accuracy is too low for a fraud model
questions.explanation: This is the accuracy paradox. When 98% of claims are legitimate, always predicting 'not fraud' gives 98% accuracy without detecting any fraud. Recall for the positive class is 0. Precision-recall metrics reveal this failure that accuracy hides.

questions.text: SMOTE generates synthetic minority-class observations by:
options: Duplicating existing minority-class observations randomly
Interpolating between a minority-class point and one of its nearest minority-class neighbours
Sampling from a Gaussian distribution fitted to the minority class
Deleting majority-class observations at random
questions.explanation: SMOTE creates synthetic points as x' = xᵢ + δ(xₙ − xᵢ) where δ ~ Uniform(0,1) and xₙ is a randomly chosen kNN in the minority class. The synthetic point lies on the line segment between xᵢ and xₙ — interpolation, not duplication or Gaussian sampling.

questions.text: You apply SMOTE to the FULL dataset (train + test) before splitting. What problem does this create?
options: SMOTE cannot run on more than 50,000 rows
Data leakage: synthetic observations near test set points inflate evaluation performance
The majority class becomes underrepresented
The recipe pipeline cannot be prepped on SMOTE-augmented data
questions.explanation: Applying SMOTE before splitting means some synthetic minority-class observations are created by interpolating between training and test set points. This leaks test set information into the training data, inflating the apparent performance. SMOTE must be applied only to the training set inside the recipe.

questions.text: Lowering the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 for a churn model will:
options: Increase both precision and recall
Decrease both precision and recall
Increase recall and decrease precision
Decrease recall and increase precision
questions.explanation: A lower threshold means more observations are classified as 'churn'. This catches more genuine churners (higher recall) but also flags more non-churners incorrectly (lower precision). The precision-recall trade-off is fundamental to imbalanced classification.

questions.text: Setting classwt = c('0' = 1, '1' = 5) in randomForest means the model treats a missed churner as 5 times more costly than a false alarm.
questions.explanation: Class weights in randomForest scale the contribution of each observation to the impurity calculation. Setting '1' = 5 means misclassifying a churner (class 1) costs 5 times as much as misclassifying a non-churner, pushing the model to correctly classify more minority-class observations.

questions.text: The Precision-Recall (PR) curve is preferred over the ROC curve for imbalanced datasets because:
options: PR-AUC is always higher than ROC-AUC
ROC-AUC is influenced by the large number of true negatives, making a poor model look good
PR curves can be plotted for any number of classes
ROC curves cannot be computed without a test set
questions.explanation: ROC-AUC includes specificity = TN / (TN + FP). When there are very many true negatives (as in an imbalanced dataset), specificity is high even for a weak model, inflating ROC-AUC. PR-AUC focuses on the minority class (precision and recall) and is not inflated by the abundance of true negatives.
